It is well recognized that population aging has implications for societies and economies. The aging society is funda mentally redefining labor markets, consumption, social networks and interaction, family structure and living, and even more so, health and welfare services [1]. Healthcare systems worldwide are challenged by the significant rise of ill health and disability due to increased life expectancy and linked frailty, and the change in the prevalence and nature of ill health from infectious diseases to complex and long-term chronic diseases [2–4]. Moreover, societal development is increasing public expectations, and ambitious new health goals are putting additional pressure on health systems to produce better health outcomes and greater social value [5, 6]. At the same time, aging has had a profound impact on “society’s capacity to provide workers to care for the pop ulation and the ability to generate income to finance this care” [1], p. 590. As a result, 20% of health spending in Europe is estimated to be allocated to services that either do not deliver the desired benefits, or are even harmful [7]. Technological advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Robotics represent a major opportunity to relieve some pressure put on the healthcare systems by societal aging [8]. In fact, the use of AI is increasing exponentially in various sectors, e.g., Business, Education, Security, and Healthcare and Nursing [9–13]. In the fifth industrial revolution, the new robotics revolves around the interactions between man and machine outside factory applications, as machines can move and act autonomously in complex and unstructured environments [14]. The robotic systems are being integrated increasingly as enablers of remote treatment and diagnosis [15, 16], to complement the human workforce in auxiliary services [17–19], as tools to improve accuracy [20, 21], and in supporting mental health and daily tasks [22–24].

The Nursing and Care sector, in particular, could gain much from the socially assistive humanoid robots (SAHRs), specifically, SAHRs robotic systems that can engage in more natural human-machine interaction using gestures, speech, facial recognition, movements, and, in general, social interaction to assist their users [25, 26]. Nursing and care staff are a critical part of healthcare and the most sig nificant section of the health profession. There are approxi mately 27.9 million nurses globally [27], and the current estimates suggest that an additional 5.9 million nurses are needed worldwide [28]. However, the integration of SAHRs in nursing and care may also have an adverse impact and disruptive potential. The more recognized issues related to nursing and care include technical barriers and technologi cal limitations, safety, privacy/data control, loss of human contact and dignity, fairness and (eco)sustainability, legiti macy and impact on the concept of care, role disruption, trust and accountability, and acceptance and negative pre conceptions [8, 29]. SAHR systems already exhibit robust and autonomous capabilities, and address initial concerns regarding physical safety around people. However, the per ception of ethical considerations related to decreased social contact, and barriers related to acceptance, such as patients’ stigmatization, social equality, and fear of the dehumaniza tion of society, have yet to be comprehended to a greater extent [29, 30].

When designing SAHRs, it is crucial to understand the diverse expectations and concerns of different kinds of stakeholders that are in direct contact with the robots [31]. Namely, successful human-robot interdependency depends firstly on the acceptance of the robot by the human users [32]. There are a number of different models for measuring technology acceptance, such as Davis’ Technology Accep tance Model (TAM) [33], the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), TAM 3 [34], the UTAUT 2 model [35], and the Almere Model [36]. Most existing studies, however, focus on long-term (elderly) care or par tial substitution of nursing activities rather than SAHRs as complementary services [8, 31, 37–39]. Additionally, ethical issues linked to SAHRs, such as those pertaining to privacy concerns, dependence on technology, loss of human contact, and decreased quality of services, are barely described in the studies [40]. Moreover, most studies’ quality of report ing and evidence is relatively low [41]. These gaps in the literature lead to oversimplification in design, and often to the delivery of unhelpful features, creating inconveniences and frustrations, preventing both patients and professionals from recognizing the added value, and hindering the suc cessful implementation of human-robot interdependency [42]. Specifically, “the implementation of a robotic system in nursing care must be seen as a complex intervention due to the number of involved stakeholders and their behaviors, the variability and number of outcomes and various inter acting components” [43], p. 2. If this complexity is ignored during the design process, robots may even be perceived as a local threat to patients’ and professionals’ independence [29, 44–46].

In general, healthcare professionals (HCPs), especially due to high workload, tend to recognize the potential value of care robots as an aid in “measuring/monitoring” (e.g., assessment of vital signs), “mobility/activity” (e.g., move ment assistance) and “safety of care” (e.g., fall prevention) [47]. However, when it comes to integrating the robotic units into fundamental aspects of nursing and care, there are still important challenges in understanding and priori tizing the collaboration between humans and robots fully [41, 48]. The barriers related to the integration of SAHRs in care routine arise especially from professionals’ ethical considerations, professional identity, and autonomy in an integrated working environment [49], which are addressed rarely.

Overall, a more anticipatory and contemporary position towards technology in nursing must be established with all stakeholders, especially HCPs and patients [50]. Hence, the present study aims to investigate (i) The general attitudes of patients towards SAHRs in the setting of in-hospital nurs ing and care, (ii) Ethical acceptability among HCPs, and (iii) Functional (technological) expectations of both HCPs and patients. The goal of this study is to gain a detailed and comprehensive insight into patients’ and HCPs’ current expectations and attitudes towards using SAHRs in nursing and care routine in the Slovenian public healthcare context, where the implementation of digital tools is particularly challenging [51]. The results of this study will broaden the existing literature and drive the design of a SAHR named “Frida” that will be deployed in clinical studies registered under ISRCTN12048782 and ISRCTN96689284, where the SAHR, patients, and HCPs will be engaging in direct contact with each other. The study has been carried out according to the study protocol [52]. To our knowledge this is one of the first studies that evaluates the acceptance of SAHRs among HCPs and patients within the same cultural and socioeconomic context at the same time. Thus, the pres ent study can serve as an enabler to develop implementation strategies aligned with patients’ and professionals’ prefer ences, and to identify the nature of tasks the SAHRs could be involved in and principles of social interaction (i.e., the virtue of which is that they can assume different roles, such as motivators or companions). Finally, the proposed study defines two structural models, one for patients and one for HCPs, to describe the associations between demographic variables, technology expectations, and ethical acceptabil ity in the acceptance of SAHRs in the in-hospital nursing and care setting.

This paper is structured as follows. Section 2 describes the study related to the expectations, ethical acceptability and acceptance of SAHR systems in care workflow as per ceived by HCPs. Section 3 describes the model of expecta tions, attitudes and acceptance as expressed by patients, and the results of both studies and limitations are discussed in Sect. 4. The concluding thoughts are outlined in Sect. 5.

HCPs have an interesting dual role in the deployment of SAHRs. First, they are the end-users of deploying SAHRs in hospital environments, meaning that, if such services are deployed, they are the ones that need to spend time with SAHRs and work in synergy with them. Second, they are also the domain experts and gatekeepers of the healthcare system, meaning that they are in the position of deciding whether the benefits of SAHRs outweigh the potential neg ative consequences, and whether their use is in line with the ethical standards of performing clinical work [53]. As a result, their views on these topics bear consequences not only for them (i.e., how they perform their work), but also for the patients (i.e., what kind of tools and services are offered to patients). Previous research suggests that HCPs, among other things, need to identify with robots as teammates, see the value of using SAHRs, feel comfortable leaving the SAHR alone with the patient, and trust that the SAHR will adhere to the expected protocols and not harm the patient [31, 54]. If these criteria are not fulfilled it is unlikely that the SAHR will be deployed, and even less likely that it will be used on a regular basis. As such, Study 1 aims to further our understanding of providers’ technology expectations (RQ1), views regarding ethical acceptability of deploying SAHRs (RQ2), and general acceptance of SAHRs in hos pital environments (RQ3), and the associations between these variables. Since it is likely that these variables are not pronounced equally in different subsamples of healthcare providers, Study 1 additionally aims to provide knowledge on demographic characteristics, including gender, age, edu cation, and occupation, that are related to healthcare pro viders’ technology expectations, ethical acceptability, and general acceptance (RQ4).

The first important determinant of SAHR acceptance are the objective technical features and, especially, the subjec tive expectations regarding the technical features of SAHR [31]. This notion can be explained via the theoretical frame work of the uncertainty reduction theory [55], which pro poses that people seek information (e.g., regarding typical behavior) before interacting with other parties to make pre dictions about others, and, consequently, reduce their uncer tainty [56]. As SAHRs are a relatively new technology that differs from other technologies due to possessing some of the human characteristics, it is suggested that they evoke a lot of uncertainty [57, 58]. Hence, individuals may feel the need to predict the behavior of social robots and build general expectations regarding SAHRs prior to interacting with them, and these expectations may, in the next step, impact their intention to accept such technology [58]. In previous literature, these subjective expectations are often operationalized in terms of “perceived usefulness”, which stems from the technology acceptance model [33]. Previ ous empirical studies of this variable suggest that perceived usefulness impacts the acceptance of robots in home envi ronments positively [59]. Similarly, a recent study by Saari and colleagues (2022) found that perceived usefulness was a significant predictor of the behavioral intention to use the “Pepper” robot (developed by SoftBank Robotics) among end-users.

Additionally, existing evidence supports the idea that perceptions regarding robots’ capabilities, such as their ability to reduce the workload, save time, and increase the quality of work, are associated significantly with the per ceived need for robots specifically among healthcare work ers as well [60, 61]. However, perceived usefulness and other variables used commonly in previous studies have a relatively narrow focus, and do not take into account the specifics and nuances of expectations regarding SAHRs, as well as the various sources people may use to develop their expectations (e.g., seeing fictional robots in mass media; [58]. As such, the present study will employ a scale that is specific to SAHRs, and differentiates between unrealistic preconceived ideas from exposure to science-fiction culture and more realistic expectations regarding the capabilities of SAHRs [62, 63], and investigate its association with the general acceptance of SAHRs.

The second predictor of SAHR acceptance that will be considered in the present study is ethical acceptability. This variable may be of the utmost importance, as the discussions about deploying SAHRs in different contexts frequently focus on ethical concerns, which is reflected through the emergence of new conferences related explicitly to robot ethics and new ethical standards in robotics and AI [64, 65]. Such debates are also prevalent in the healthcare context, where critics of implementing SAHRs often highlight their potential threat to humane and dignified care. More specific ethical concerns include minimization of human contact, deprivation of affective and emotional warmth, reducing the human being to an object, privacy [44, 66], but also pos sible emotional deception and emotional attachment to the robot [64]. Previous empirical studies suggest that ethical and privacy concerns affect use intention and general accep tance significantly and negatively [67, 68]. Similar results were also found in a study that employed a mixed sample of patients and HCPs; specifically, the authors found support for their hypothesis that ethical concerns have a negative effect on the intention to use home healthcare robots [60]. However, previous studies largely lack a more differenti ated analysis of the ethical issues surrounding social robot ics [66]. Hence, not much is known about the association between healthcare providers’ views on different aspects of ethical acceptability (e.g., acceptability for use, accept ability of human-like interaction, and acceptability of nonhuman appearance; [69] and general acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environments. The present study thus seeks to address this gap in the literature.

Lastly, general acceptance of SAHRs in hospital envi ronments may differ between individuals with different demographic characteristics, such as age and education level. Although this varies between different contexts, older individuals are generally less comfortable with new tech nology than younger people. They are also more distrust ful and fearful of new technology than younger individuals [70, 71]. As a matter of fact, several previous studies have found a significant negative association between age and the intention to use social robots (e.g., [72]. Studies conducted on healthcare providers are scarce and inconclusive, but overall suggest that the relationship between age and accep tance may be different than in the general population. For example, Andtfolk and colleagues (2021), who employed a mixed sample of healthcare providers and patients, have recently found that older individuals are more likely to favor the use of humanoid robots in healthcare than younger indi viduals. Similarly, Turja and colleagues (2018) report that younger age predicted a lower level of robot acceptance at work among HCPs. On the other hand, previous studies conducted among healthcare providers and other popula tions suggest rather uniformly that higher education is asso ciated with greater acceptance of SAHRs [73–75]. Besides age and education, the occupation of HCPs may also be important. While not many studies investigated the role of occupation in the acceptance of SAHRs in hospital envi ronments, the existing studies do suggest that physicians, nurses, and other healthcare workers, such as physiothera pists and social workers, differ in this aspect [39, 76].

The present study aims to integrate the variables described above (i.e., demographic variables, technology expectations, ethical acceptability) into a comprehensive model (Fig. 1) that could help us explain the differences in HCPs’ general acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environ ments. The variables are ordered from the most general indi vidual characteristics (i.e., age and education1) to variables related to how the SAHR is perceived and what is expected of it, views on the ethical acceptability of using SAHRs in hospital environments, to the final variable, general accep tance of SAHRs. Since demographic variables, technology expectations, and ethical acceptability are all associated with general acceptance, they are also likely associated with each other. As such, these paths will also be explored.

A total of 651 employees of a regional Clinical Cen tre started filling out the study. After excluding partici pants who dropped out during the study, the final sample included 490 participants. The average age of participants was 42.56 years (SD = 11.02), ranging from 21 to 66 years. Most of the sample was employed as (nursing) care staff (41.02%), fol lowed by doctors and specialists (21.02%), administration (12.45%), and support staff (e.g., IT, maintenance; 3.47%), while approximately one-fifth of the sample (22.04%) responded with ‘other’. Since the support staff subgroup is rather small, it was merged with participants who responded with ‘other’ in further analyses. Regarding the educational level, most participants completed secondary education (26.73%) or had a Bachelor’s degree (26.73%), followed by a Master’s degree (22.24%), specialization or scien tific Master’s Degree (15.51%), lower tertiary education (5.10%), and a Doctoral degree (3.67%).

Providers completed questionnaires regarding their tech nology-specific expectations towards the SAHRs, ethical acceptability, general acceptance of SAHRs in the hospital environment, and questions regarding their socio-demo graphic characteristics. Technology-specific expectations towards SAHRs were measured with the Technology-Specific Expectations Scale (TSES) [62]. The scale consists of 10 items (e.g., “I think I will be able to interact with the robot.”), which are answered on a four-point Likert-type scale ranging from one (“very low expectation”) to four (“very high expectation”). The items form two subscales, namely, Capabilities (i.e., expectations that users have towards the robot’s capabili ties; five items) and Fictional view (i.e., impressions created mostly by sci-fi culture; five items), both with good internal consistency (α = 0.77 and α = 0.75, respectively). TSES was originally developed for the assessment of children’s expec tations towards a robotic tutor and validated on the sample of 14–16 year old students [62]. Nevertheless, the content of items suggests its suitability for them to be used within a sample of adults as well.

The ethical acceptability of the SAHR was measured with the Ethical Acceptability Scale (EAS) [69]. The scale consists of 12 items (e.g., “It is ethically acceptable that social robots are used in healthcare.”), answered on fourpoint Likert-type scale ranging from one (“strongly dis agree”) to four (“strongly agree”). The items form three subscales, namely, Ethical acceptability for use (i.e., the extent to which participants believe the use of social robots is ethically acceptable; five items), Ethical acceptability of human-like interaction (i.e., the extent to which partici pants believe that it is ethically acceptable for social robots to replace human interactions; four items), and Ethical acceptability of non-human appearance (i.e., the extent to which participants believe that it is ethically acceptable for social robots to look like objects, imaginary creatures, or animals; three items), all three with good internal consis tency (α = 0.86, α = 0.72, and 0.76, respectively). The EAS was originally developed for the assessment of the accept ability of social robots to be used in healthcare of children with autism. Therefore, some items of the scale are contentspecific for this population, and were adapted to reflect the use of SAHRs more generally (e.g., “It is ethically accept able that social robots are used in therapy for children with autism.” was reworded to “It is ethically acceptable to use social robots in clinical care.”). TSES and EAS were adapted to the Slovenian language using the translation-back translation method [77]. The internal structure and internal consistency of all the ques tionnaires were assessed and are reported in the Results section.

To assess the general acceptance of SAHRs in a hospi tal environment, the providers answered four dichotomous questions (answered by marking “yes” or “no” to indicate the (dis)agreement), constructed specifically for this study. The items were: (1) “Would you like to be employed at a hospital where a robot is part of the medical team?”, (2) “Do you think that the robot could help patients fill out hos pital records (e.g., medications patients are taking, a record of basic information such as gender, age, address, etc.)?”, (3) “Do you think the robot could answer the patient’s addi tional questions regarding treatment?”, and (4) “Would you agree that the robot helps and guides or takes over a part of your work/time you dedicate to the patient during rehabili tation after surgery (e.g., additional breathing exercises)?”. Additionally, participants were asked to provide the infor mation on their gender, age, occupation, and educational level.

Data were collected amongst the regional hospital’s employ ees. All employees working in the participating medical institution aged between 18 and 65 years were eligible to participate in the study. Hospital’s employees were invited to participate in the study via e-mail that included informa tion about the study and a link to the survey. Those who visited the link, first filled out the informed consent and then proceeded to fill out the questionnaires described earlier. Following the study protocol [52], participants’ data were collected for four months since the beginning of the study, aiming to reach the desired sample size of 500 participants, which represents a generally sufficient sample for struc tural equation modeling analyses [78]. Ethical approval was obtained from the Medical Ethics Commission of the UKC Maribor (UKCM-MB-KME-40/21).

section: 2 Study 1: Healthcare Professionals > 2.2 Methods > 2.2.4 Statistical Analyses
text: Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 8.0. First, participants with incomplete data (i.e., those who dropped out) were excluded from the analyses. In the next step, we checked the data for outliers and assessed other assumptions of the planned analyses (e.g., normal dis tribution). As no issues were detected, we proceeded with calculating the basic descriptive statistics and bivariate cor relations between variables. In the next step, we performed analyses of variance for the assessment of the potential dif ferences regarding technology expectations, ethical accept ability, and acceptance of SAHRs in a hospital environment between different occupational groups. Where significant differences were obtained, we performed post-hoc tests to assess further the pairwise differences between means in the aforementioned constructs. In the final step of analyses, the model was tested using structural equation modeling (SEM) and the robust maxi mum likelihood estimator (MLR). All constructs that consist of multiple items were modeled as latent factors. The model fit was assessed with the χ2 goodness of fit test, Comparative Fit Index (CFI ≥ 0.90 recommended), Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA ≤ 0.08 recommended) and Standardized Root Mean Residual (SRMR ≤ 0.08 rec ommended; Kline, 2005). Standardized estimates for path coefficients, interpreted as regression coefficients, were cal culated for all the proposed relationships in the model and the relevant indirect effects to test for mediation.

Age was generally associated weakly positively with technology expectations regarding SAHRs, ethical acceptability and general acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environments. The only exception was the non-human appearance subscale of ethical acceptability. Providers’ education levels generally exhibited similar, but stronger, correlations with the vari ables of interest. text: Additionally, the descriptive statistics generally revealed that both fictional view and capabilities (subdimensions of technology expectations) were pronounced similarly in this sample. On the other hand, ethical acceptability for use was pronounced higher than the remaining two subdimen sions of ethical acceptability. A more detailed look at the items that constitute the “acceptance” dimension revealed that 67.60% of providers are willing to work in a hospital where a SAHR is also a part of the healthcare team, 65.50% believe that the SAHR could help patients fill out the paper work, 58.80% believe that the SAHR could help with reha bilitation after an operative procedure, while only 28.80% believe that the SAHR could answer patients’ questions regarding their treatment. Following our research questions, we also analyzed whether technology expectations, ethical acceptability and general acceptance differed based on the providers’ occupa tion. These results are presented in Fig. 2, while detailed results can be found in Supplementary materials (Table S1).

section: 2 Study 1: Healthcare Professionals > 2.3 Results > 2.3.1 Descriptive Statistics, Bivariate Correlations and Group Comparisons
text: The figure shows that technology expectations, ethi cal acceptability and general acceptance were generally the lowest among nurses, while the highest means were generally found in the subsample of doctors. Differences between occupations were significant in the case of all vari ables except the fictional view subdimension of technology expectations, and the effect sizes were small to medium. As shown by the Hochberg’s GT2 post-hoc test, perceptions regarding the capabilities of SAHRs differed significantly only between nurses and physicians (p = .008**). The ethi cal acceptability of human-like interaction differed signifi cantly between administrators and physicians (p = .003**), nurses and physicians p = < 0.001**, and physicians and others (p = .008**). Meanwhile, the ethical acceptability of non-human appearances differed significantly between administrators and physicians p = < 0.001**, nurses and physicians p = < 0.001**, nurses and others (p = .011*), and physicians and others (p = .005**). For the remaining pairwise comparisons, we used the Games-Howell posthoc test. This test revealed that ethical acceptability for use differed significantly between administrators and phy sicians p = < 0.001**, nurses and physicians p = < 0.001**, nurses and others (p = .014*), and physicians and others (p = .002**). Lastly, the general acceptance differed signifi cantly between administrators and physicians (p = .013*), nurses and physicians p = < 0.001**, and physicians and others (p = .025*).

section: 2 Study 1: Healthcare Professionals > 2.3 Results > 2.3.2 Testing the Structural Model
text: In the next step, we established appropriate measurement models of the latent variables included in our theoretical Fig. 3 Results of structural equation modeling in the sample of HCPs. model (see Fig. 1). After allowing correlated measurement errors between a few pairs of items within the same sub scale, all measurement models exhibited a satisfactory fit (CFI = > 0.92, RMSEA = < 0.08, SRMR = < 0.05). Accord ing to the factor analyses, items belonged to the dimen sions proposed by previous authors, and the loadings were between 0.44 and 0.75 in the case of TSES, between 0.64 and 0.95 in the case of EAS, and between 0.54 and 0.82 in the case of general acceptance. Our structural model, in which we allowed factors from the same scale (e.g., fictional view and capabilities) to covary, showed a good fit of the data: χ2(317) = 804.89, p = < 0.001**, CFI = 0.93, RMSEA = 0.06 (90% CI: 0.05, 0.06), SRMR = 0.05. The structural model is shown in the Figure below (Fig. 3), where the significant paths are marked with a black line and non-significant paths with a dotted gray line. In the structural model, age predicted fictional view (β = 0.14**) and capabilities (β = 0.14**) significantly, while education level predicted capabilities (β = 0.11*) signifi cantly, but not fictional view. On the other hand, age was not a statistically significant predictor of aspects related to ethical acceptability, while education level predicted ethi cal acceptability for use (β = 0.20***), ethical acceptability of human-like interaction (β = 0.16**), and ethical accept ability of non-human appearance significantly (β = 0.32**). Neither age nor education level were significant predictors of general acceptance.

section: 2 Study 1: Healthcare Professionals > 2.3 Results > 2.3.2 Testing the Structural Model
text: Both aspects of technology expectations were generally positively associated with aspects of ethical acceptability. Specifically, fictional view predicted ethical acceptability for use (β = 0.34**) and ethical acceptability of human-like interaction (β = 0.27*), but not ethical acceptability of nonhuman appearance. Capabilities, on the other hand, predicted all three aspects significantly, namely, ethical acceptability for use (β = 0.41**), ethical acceptability of human-like interaction (β = 0.47**), and ethical acceptability of nonhuman appearance (β = 0.46**). Neither fictional view nor capabilities predicted general acceptance significantly. Lastly, ethical acceptability for use (β = 0.65**) and ethical acceptability of human-like interaction (β = 0.29*) predicted general acceptance significantly, while ethical acceptability of non-human appearance did not. Overall, the structural model explained about 86.00% of variance in the general acceptance of SAHRs in a hospital environment (R2 = 0.86**). As neither demographic variables nor technology expec tations predicted acceptance directly, we also investigated whether these variables exert an indirect effect on accep tance, via aspects of ethical acceptability. This is true in the case of education. Education level exhibits a positive indirect effect on general acceptance via ethical accept ability for use (point estimate = 0.13**), but not via ethical acceptability for human-like interaction and ethical accept ability of non-human appearance. Fictional view also exerts an indirect effect on acceptance via ethical acceptability for use (point estimate = 0.22**), but not via other aspects of ethical acceptability. Similarly, capabilities also exhibited an indirect effect on acceptance via ethical acceptability for use (point estimate = 0.27**), but not via other aspects of ethical acceptability. On the other hand, age did not exert an indirect effect on general acceptance via any aspect of ethical acceptability.

When the goal is to implement SAHRs into hospital envi ronments, acceptance of this idea on the providers’ side is a necessary but not sufficient condition; of course, the final end-users, in this case, patients, also need to recog nize their value, and be open to the idea of interacting with them. However, this is often not the case. Patients may have various concerns regarding the implementation of SAHRs, resulting in low acceptance [79]. In fact, a large-scale sur vey conducted by the European Commission [80] reports that a large proportion of EU citizens are against the use of robots within healthcare, although acceptance can vary, depending on the proposed function of the robot [70]. More over, a recent study investigating the change in attitudes towards robots in the European Union between 2012 and 2017 reports that public opinion regarding robots exhibits a negative trend [81]. As such, research that can improve our understanding of this low acceptance, particularly in the healthcare context, is needed to advance the debate regard ing the main barriers on the patients’ side, and take the nec essary steps to reduce them (e.g., appropriate design, raising awareness regarding the actual capabilities of SAHRs, preparing campaigns aimed at changing the attitudes of the general public). Hence, Study 2 aims to further our understanding of patients’ technology expectations (RQ1), negative attitudes towards SAHRs (RQ2), and general acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environments (RQ3), and the associations between these variables. As in Study 1, we will also investigate the relationship between demographic characteristics, specifically gender, age, and education, and patients’ technology expectations, negative attitudes, and general acceptance (RQ4).

The potential role of technology expectations is already explained in Sect. 2.1. As in the case of HCPs, patients are also inclined to form subjective expectations regarding the technical features of SAHRs to reduce uncertainty prior to interacting with them [31, 55]. Previous studies suggest that patients’ performance expectations are generally lower than clinicians [82], and that variables that at least partially cap ture these expectations are associated with robot acceptance in the healthcare context [31, 59]. However, studies inves tigating subjective technical expectations more comprehen sively and specifically within this population are lacking. Several well-known theories and models emphasize the associations between attitudes, behavioral intentions, and behavior, with two notable examples being the theory of reasoned action [83] and the theory of planned behavior [84]. Meta-analyses support the notion that such models can predict behavioral intentions and behavior in various con texts, with average correlations between attitudes and inten tions being positive and intermediate in strength [85–87]. Hence, it is likely that individuals’ favorable or unfavor able evaluations of interactions with SAHRs and SAHRs as objects are an essential determinant of their acceptance as well. In fact, previous studies have already established this to some degree; the study by de Graaf and Allouch (2013), conducted on a sample of 60 students, reports a significant positive correlation between attitudes towards social robots and use intention. Similarly, Heerink and colleagues (2008) reported that older people accept robots to a higher degree if they believe that they will enjoy situations of interaction with them. However, associations between attitudes towards SAHRs and their acceptance in the healthcare context are, at the moment, not as well-understood. This is particularly true once we consider specific sets of attitudes, such as those measured by the Negative Attitudes towards Robots Scale (NARS; [88]).

Lastly, patients’ demographic factors, particularly age and education level, may also be important. While studies among this population group are rare, studies conducted in other contexts generally suggest that older individuals are less likely to accept SAHRs [72, 75], while individuals with higher education are more likely to accept SAHRs [73]. The second study thus aims to build and test a compre hensive model (Fig. 4) using the variables related to patients’ acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environments, specifically, demographic variables, technology expectations, and nega tive attitudes. The variables are ordered sequentially from the most general demographic characteristics, via SAHRrelated expectations and attitudes, to general acceptance of SAHRs.

A total of 397 patients of a regional Clinical Center started filling out the study. After excluding participants who dropped out during the study, the final sample included 371 participants. Slightly more than half of the sample identi fied as male (56.06%), while others identified as female (43.94%). The average age of participants was 59.56 years (SD = 14.69). Regarding the educational level, the major ity of the sample completed secondary education (63.07%), followed by primary education (12.94%), lower tertiary education (11.59%), a Master’s degree (6.20%), a Bach elor’s degree (4.58%), specialization or a scientific Master’s degree (1.35%), and a Doctoral degree (0.27%).

Patients completed questionnaires regarding their tech nology-specific expectations and their negative attitudes towards the SAHRs, questions on the general acceptance of SAHRs in the hospital environment, and provided informa tion on their socio-demographic characteristics. As in the sample of providers, TSES [62], already described in Sect. 2.2.2., was used for the assessment of technology-specific expectations of patients towards the SAHRs. Negative attitudes towards the SAHRs were measured with NARS [88]. The scale consists of 14 items (e.g., “I would feel very nervous just standing in front of a robot.”), answered on a four-point Likert-type scale from one (“strongly disagree”) to four (“strongly agree”). The items form three subscales, namely, Negative attitudes toward situations of interaction with robots (i.e., negative attitudes and anxiety toward situations of using robots; six items), Negative attitudes toward social influence of robots (i.e., negative attitudes and anxiety toward social influence of robots; five items), and Negative attitudes toward emotions in interaction with robots (i.e., negative attitudes related to emotions evoked in interaction with robots; three items). The first two subscales presented good internal consistency (α = 0.75 and α = 0.78, respectively), while the internal con sistency of the three-item subscale was lower (α = 0.65; Nomura et al., 2006). To assess the acceptance of SAHRs in a hospital envi ronment, patients answered four dichotomous questions (answered by marking “yes” or “no” to indicate (dis)agree ment), constructed specifically for this study. The items were (1) “Would you like to be treated in a hospital where a robot is part of themedical team?”, (2) “Would you agree to talk to a robot that would answer any additional ques tions you may have about your treatment?”, (3) “Would you agree to have a robot measure your body temperature?”, and (4) “Would you agree that the robot helps you addition ally and guides you during rehabilitation after surgery or recovery from illness (e.g., additional breathing exercises, recreational activities)?”. Additionally, participants were asked to provide the information on their gender, age, and educational level.

The TSES and NARS were adapted to the Slovenian lan guage using the translation-back translation method [77]. The internal structure and internal consistency of all the questionnaires were assessed and are reported in the Results section.

Patients hospitalized in the regional Clinical Center at the time of the survey aged 18 years or above were eligible to participate, excluding patients hospitalized at the Depart ment of Psychiatry, Clinic for Gynecology and Perinatology, or the Pediatric Clinic. Patients were invited to participate in the study by the hospital staff. They were informed about the study’s intent, procedure, foreseen analyses, dissemination strategy, along with the voluntary and anonymous nature of their potential participation, and the right to terminate the Table 2 Descriptive statistics and bivariate correlations: Patients participation at any time without any consequences. Patients who signed the informed consent responded to the battery of questionnaires described above in a digital format using a tablet provided by the hospital staff. As with the sample of providers, data were collected for four months since the beginning of the study [52]. Ethical approval was, as for the study of providers, obtained from the Medical Ethics Com mission of the UKC Maribor (UKCM-MB-KME-40/21).

The statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 8.0. In the first step participants with incom plete data (i.e., those who dropped out) were excluded from the analyses. Second, we checked the data for outliers and assessed other assumptions of the planned analyses (e.g., normal distribution). As no issues were detected, we then proceeded with calculating the basic descriptive statistics and bivariate correlations between the variables. In the final step of analysis, the model was again tested using SEM and MLR as the estimator. The model fit was assessed with the same criteria as those described in Sect. 2.2.4.

section: 3 Study 2: Patients > 3.3 Results > 3.3.1 Descriptive Statistics and Bivariate Correlations
text: We calculated the basic descriptive statistics (Means, Stan dard Deviations) and bivariate correlations between all pairs of variables. As can be seen in Table 2, gender was associ ated significantly only with one aspect of technology expec tations, specifically the capabilities subdimension. The correlation was weak and negative, indicating that female patients had lower expectations regarding the capabilities of SAHRs. Age was associated positively with negative atti tudes toward situations of interaction with robots and nega tive attitudes toward the social influence of robots, implying that these aspects of negative attitudes increase with age. Specifically, education level was related positively to the capabilities subdimension of tech nology expectations, related negatively to negative attitudes toward situations of interaction with robots and negative attitudes toward the social influence of robots, and related positively to the general acceptance of SAHRs in hospi tal environments. section: 3 Study 2: Patients > 3.3 Results > 3.3.1 Descriptive Statistics and Bivariate Correlations
text: Moreover, the descriptive statistics of both technology expectations dimensions show that capabilities were pro nounced higher than the fictional view. Among the different aspects of negative attitudes towards SAHRs, the highest mean was observed in the case of negative attitudes toward the social influence of robots, and the lowest mean was observed in the case of negative attitudes toward situations of interaction with robots. A more detailed look at the items that constitute the “acceptance” dimension revealed that 85.40% would agree to have a robot measure their body temperature, 66.30% would agree that the robot helps them during rehabilitation after surgery, 61.50% would agree to be treated in a hospital where a robot is part of the team, and 60.1% would agree to talk with a robot that would answer their questions regarding treatment.

section: 3 Study 2: Patients > 3.3 Results > 3.3.2 Testing the Structural Model
text: Before testing the structural model, we first established measurement models of the latent variables included in our theoretical model (see Fig. 4). However, to achieve a good fit of the measurement models, we had to make two notable adjustments. First, item #5 (“I think the robot will be similar to the robots I see in movies.”) had to be excluded from the fictional view subscale of TSES, as it exhibited a low load ing (0.20). Second, item #14 (“I feel that in the future soci ety will be dominated by robots.”) had to be excluded from the social influence subscale of NARS, as it exhibited a low and negative loading (-0.04). After making these adjust ments and allowing correlated measurement errors between a few pairs of items within the same subscale, all mea surement models exhibited satisfactory fit (CFI = > 0.93, RMSEA = < 0.08, SRMR = < 0.05). According to the fac tor analyses, the remaining items belonged to the dimen sions proposed by previous authors, and the loadings were between 0.58 and 0.71 in the case of TSES, between 0.51 and 0.76 in the case of NARS, and between 0.53 and 0.83 in the case of general acceptance. Our structural model, in which we again allowed fac tors from the same questionnaire to covary, showed a good fit of the data: χ2(314) = 630.83, p = < 0.001**, CFI = 0.90, RMSEA = 0.05 (90% CI: 0.05, 0.06), SRMR = 0.06. The structural model is shown in the figure below (Fig. 5), where the significant paths are marked with a black line and nonsignificant paths with a dotted gray line.

section: 3 Study 2: Patients > 3.3 Results > 3.3.2 Testing the Structural Model
text: In the structural model, age predicted fictional view sig nificantly (β = − 0.12*) but not capabilities, while educa tion level predicted capabilities significantly (β = 0.14*) but not fictional view. Furthermore, age was not a statistically significant predictor of negative attitudes toward SAHRs, while education level predicted negative attitudes toward the social influence of robots significantly (β = − 0.14*), but not other aspects of negative attitudes toward SAHRs. Nei ther age nor education level predicted general acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environments significantly. A more detailed look at technology expectations and their structural associations with other variables reveals that fictional view was not associated significantly with negative attitudes toward SAHRs, nor general acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environments. Capabilities, on the other hand, predicted negative attitudes toward situations of interaction with robots (β = − 0.56**) and negative attitudes toward emotions in interaction with robots significantly (β = − 0.46**), but not negative attitudes toward the social influ ence of robots. Patients with higher expectations regarding the capabilities of SAHRs also exhibited higher general acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environments (β = 0.53*). Lastly, negative attitudes toward the social influence of robots predicted general acceptance of SAHRs significantly (β = − 0.43*), while negative attitudes towards situations of interaction with robots and negative attitudes toward emotions in interaction with robots did not. Altogether, the structural model explained about 68.00% of variance in general acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environments (R2 = 0.68**). We also investigated whether the demographic variables (age, education level) and fictional view exerted an indirect effect on the general acceptance of SAHRs in hospital envi ronments (via negative attitudes toward SAHRs). This was not the case neither with age nor education level. Mediation analyses also revealed that fictional view did not exert a sig nificant indirect effect on general acceptance.

The aim of the paper was to describe the expectations and attitudes towards implementing SAHRs into a nursing and care routine of a hospital. The results - which will also be used to guide the functional design of Frida’s behavior and Fig. 5 Results of structural equation modeling in the sample of patients capabilities, when deployed in the operational environ ment in studies registered under ISRCTN12048782 and ISRCTN96689284 – provide critical knowledge that unrav els stakeholders’ perceptions and acceptance of SAHRs, and may guide their deployment. Namely, successful deploy ment of SAHRs in a nursing and care setting depends firstly on the acceptance of the robots by the humans who are in direct contact with the robots [31, 32], i.e., HCPs (Study 1) and patients (Study 2). Overall, the majority of participants (HCPs and patients) expressed a positive attitude towards the human-robot interdependency in a nursing and care rou tine during hospitalization. Our results are consistent with some of the previous studies implying that there is a gen erally positive attitude towards the use of SAHRs in nurs ing and care routine [73, 76, 89]. For example, 60.1% of patients would agree to talk with a robot that would answer their questions regarding treatment. Moreover, 67.6% of HCPs would be willing to work alongside an SAHR.

Through our analyses of the associations between background variables (age, gender and education), and expectations and attitudes of patients and HCPs (i.e., admin istrators, nurses and clinicians), we extend the knowledge of previous research by highlighting how an individual’s role in the healthcare system (i.e., patient versus employee) defines their model of general acceptance. As highlighted by this study, the general acceptance of SAHRs by HCPs is driven strongly by ethical acceptability (use, human-like interaction). Consistent with previous research [31, 76], education plays an important, yet indirect, role in explain ing the general acceptance of HCPs by exerting a significant impact via ethical acceptability for use. When analyzing the model of general acceptance of SAHRs in the sample of patients, a strong association was observed with the social influence aspect of negative attitudes and realistic expec tations regarding capabilities. Interestingly, education is a significant predictor of both aspects, and is also correlated significantly with acceptance, but does not exert a direct or indirect effect on acceptance via negative attitudes and tech nology expectation. Surprisingly, however, neither gender nor age were observed to have any direct or indirect impact on the general acceptance of SAHR among patients. In fact, even on the correlational level, age was only observed to be weakly associated with the general acceptance of SAHR among HCPs. This observation partially contradicts the findings in related research, where it was observed that age, especially among the patient population, represents a key predictor, and that acceptance of SAHRs decreases with age [47, 70, 71, 73].

Similarly, as reported by Backonja and colleagues [90], our study dispels the perception that age is the common denominator of technological acceptance, i.e., younger adults are easily engaged with robotic (and other) technolo gies, whereas older adults need more persuasion. In fact, regardless of age, it seems that both patients and HCPs gen erally welcome the use of SAHRs in hospital environments, but struggle to accept technologies in specific domains that may hinder or change the already established social balances in healthcare. Namely, over 85% of patients would agree to have a robot measure their body temperature, whereas only 60% would be comfortable to talk with a robot that would answer their questions regarding treatment, and only 29% of HCPs believe that the SAHR could answer patients’ ques tions regarding their treatment. This further supports the notion that anthropomorphic characteristics alone do not influence acceptance and trust towards AI devices [91], and that most professionals still have doubts regarding the inter action quality SAHRs can deliver. As such, it seems that exposition to information/knowledge, as well as to actual robots at work or at home, has significantly (and positively) changed the perception of robotic technologies, but there are still certain areas of use that evoke fear and uncertainty. To understand the mechanism that drives professionals’ and patients’ acceptance of SAHRs better, the following subsec tions discuss both structural models in detail.

section: 4 Discussion > 4.1 Discussion on the Structural Model for Healthcare Professionals
text: In Study 1, we aimed to integrate the variables of technolog ical expectations, ethical acceptability, and general accep tance, together with some demographic characteristics, into a structural model. The results generally support our expectations of the relationships between them, and provide some additional opportunities to be explored in the future research. As previous studies suggest, general acceptance of SAHRs is determined by (at least) the objective technical features of SAHRs and subjective expectations regarding these features (e.g., [31], and the views on ethical accept ability (e.g.,[44, 66], while it may also differ depending on different demographic characteristics [70–73, 75, 76]. Therefore, in Study 1, we aimed to explore the technology expectations of HCPs, their views regarding ethical accept ability of deploying SAHRs and general acceptance of SAHRs in the hospital environment, and the relation among demographic characteristics and technology expectations, ethical acceptability and general acceptance of SAHRs. Our findings, explored by the correlations among variables and comparing the Means between occupational groups, gen erally support the findings of previous studies, especially when explored via the structural model of the main vari ables of the present study. The proposed structural model fitted the data well, and explained a large majority of the variance (i.e., 86.00%) in the general acceptance of SAHRs in the hospital environ ment. Even though previous studies suggest that the expec tations towards SAHRs determine their general acceptance [31], our model did not exhibit any significant direct effects of technology expectations on the general acceptance of SAHRs. However, these expectations proved to predict eth ical acceptability significantly positively, i.e., the fictional view predicted ethical acceptability for use and of humanlike interaction positively, while capabilities predicted all three dimensions of ethical acceptability positively (i.e., ethical acceptability for use, human-like interaction, and non-human appearance). Then, both dimensions of technol ogy expectations predicted general acceptance of SAHRs significantly positively by indirect effect via ethical accept ability for use. While previous studies generally employed concepts of perceived usefulness [33] and other less spe cific definitions of expectations towards SAHRs, and found important effects of them on the general acceptance of SAHRs, our results suggest that, when specifically exploring technological expectations in the form of fictional view and capabilities of SAHRs, these do not present direct effects on their general acceptance. However, they do prove significant relationships through ethical acceptability of SAHRs. Two dimensions of ethical acceptability (i.e., ethical acceptabil ity for use and human-like interaction), further on, predicted the general acceptance of SAHRs significantly positively. This finding specifically supports previous notions on the importance of the ethical aspects of employing SAHRs generally and in the context of healthcare (Alaiad & Zhou, 2014; Etemad-Sajadi et al., 2022; Lutz & Tamò-Larrieux, 2021).

section: 4 Discussion > 4.1 Discussion on the Structural Model for Healthcare Professionals
text: Additionally, we explored the demographic characteris tics of HCPs and their relations to technology expectations, ethical acceptability, and general acceptance. While age and educational level proved no significant direct effects on general acceptance, some interesting results were obtained regarding their effects on technical expectations and ethical acceptability. According to previous studies, age generally demonstrates a negative association with trust in technology (Broadbent et al., 2009; Czaja & Sharit, 1998), and with the intention to use social robots [72]. However, in our study, the age of participants predicted both dimensions of technology expectations significantly, suggesting that older individuals have higher expectations regarding the SAHRs’ capabili ties, and also have more pronounced expectations shaped by sci-fi culture than younger participants. On the other hand, age did not predict any of the dimensions of ethical acceptability, nor general acceptance of SAHRs. Regard ing educational level, previous studies suggest its positive relationship with the acceptance of SAHRs [73–75]. The educational level in our study predicted the fictional view of SAHRs positively, and also all three dimensions of ethi cal acceptability, and, while there was no direct effect of educational level and the acceptance of SAHR, there was a significant positive indirect effect between these concepts via ethical acceptability for use. Interesting results also emerged from the comparison of technology expectations, ethical acceptability, and general acceptance among occupational groups, generally sup porting previous notions on the differences between dif ferent groups of HCPs in the acceptance of SAHRs [39, 76]. Indeed, general acceptance of SAHRs was the high est among physicians and lowest among nurses. Similarly, expectations on capabilities, and all three dimensions of ethical acceptability were highest among physicians and lowest among nurses (while there were no differences in the fictional view).

section: 4 Discussion > 4.2 Discussion on the Structural Model for Patients
text: In Study 2, we focused on the exploration of the general acceptance of SAHRs and related concepts from the per spective of patients. While studies that specifically tackle patients’ acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environments are rare, the existing literature from similar contexts sug gests that general acceptance of SAHRs may be influenced by variables capturing subjective expectations and attitudes towards social robots [59, 92, 93], and may vary based on demographic variables such as age and education [70, 72, 73]. Therefore, in Study 2, we aimed to explore the tech nology expectations of patients, their negative attitudes towards social robots, and general acceptance of SAHRs in the hospital environment, as well as the association between these variables and patients’ demographic characteristics. Our findings, obtained with correlational analyses and struc tural equation modeling, are generally in line with previous research, but provide a more nuanced understanding of the state of these variables and the associations between them.

section: 4 Discussion > 4.2 Discussion on the Structural Model for Patients
text: The proposed structural model exhibited an acceptable fit to the data and explained a large portion of variance (i.e., 68.00%) in the general acceptance of SAHRs in the hospital environment. Within the model, capabilities (i.e., an aspect of technology expectations) predicted two dimensions of negative attitudes towards SAHRs as well as general accep tance of SAHRs significantly. These associations support the previous findings on the relationship between subjec tive expectations and acceptance of social robots [31, 59]. While the other aspect of technology expectations, fictional view, generally exhibited similar correlations (suggesting that individuals with a more pronounced fictional view have lower negative attitudes and higher acceptance of SAHRs), it did not emerge as a significant predictor of acceptance, neither directly nor indirectly (via negative attitudes). These results suggest that individuals’ views of realistic capabili ties of the SAHR determine acceptance to a higher degree compared to individuals’ fictional views stemming from sci ence fiction movies or series, which overstate robots’ physi cal and cognitive abilities [58]. Next, negative attitudes toward social influence of robots predicted patients’ gen eral acceptance of SAHRs in hospital environments sig nificantly. This finding generally supports the notion that negative attitudes play an important part in individuals’ behavioral intentions in general, as well as specifically the intention to use an SAHR [36, 85, 92]. However, this might not be the case equally for all types of negative attitudes towards SAHRs.

section: 4 Discussion > 4.2 Discussion on the Structural Model for Patients
text: In our study, the other two aspects of nega tive attitudes (negative attitudes towards situations of inter action with robots and negative attitudes toward emotions in interaction with robots) exhibited similar correlations with the focal outcome, but did not exhibit a significant unique predictive value in the structural model. Interestingly, the social influence aspect of negative attitudes was also the most pronounced and least dispersed in our sample, sug gesting that individuals might be rather uniformly afraid of the potential of SAHRs to influence others and dominate the society (compared to simply interacting with the robot and facing a robot that has emotions). As these outcomes are not realistic in the context of healthcare, where the SARHs are proposed to be a solution that can complement the exist ing protocols and reduce employees’ workload (instead of replacing them), such attitudes should be tackled in the future to increase the overall acceptance of SAHRs. Lastly, we explored the demographic characteristics of patients and their relations to technology expectations, neg ative attitudes, and general acceptance. On the correlation level, education exhibited a weak positive association with acceptance, implying that acceptance of SAHRs in hospi tal environments increases slightly with patients’ levels of education, but neither age nor education exerted a signifi cant (direct or indirect) effect on general acceptance in the structural model. Regardless, they still play an interesting and important role in the model, as both variables exhib ited significant associations with certain aspects of technol ogy expectations and negative attitudes. Specifically, age emerged as a significant predictor of fictional view, while education proved to be a significant predictor of capabilities and negative attitudes toward the social influence of robots (i.e., two variables that contribute significantly to the overall acceptance). Such results are, hence, only partially in line with previous studies highlighting the importance of age and education in this context [70, 72, 73].

The findings of the present study should be interpreted in the light of some limitations. While data were collected randomly among all eligible participants, it is possible that individuals with strong positive (or strong negative) atti tudes were more inclined to volunteer and consent to par ticipate in the study. This could lead to a bias and limit the generalizability of our results (although it is worth noting that the results do show considerable variability of the focal variables). Furthermore, on the level of conceptualization and measurement, studies 1 and 2 were not completely aligned, which makes it more difficult to compare their results directly. First, to ensure that only the most relevant variables were measured in each sample (to keep the study as short as possible and reduce drop-out), we assessed ethi cal acceptance in the sample of HCPs, while we assessed negative attitudes in the sample of patients. Second, in the sample of patients, the translated version of TSES did not correspond completely with the factorial structure proposed by the original authors (i.e., one item had to be excluded due to low factor loading), which hinders the possibility of com paring the results obtained in this sample with the HCP’s results, and also with other studies using the same ques tionnaire. One additional limitation might be that the actual SAHR was not presented to the participants.

Therefore, they were not completely informed about the characteristics of the robot that would be present in the situations they were providing their opinions on. However, they were all aware that the robot would be humanoid and of the tasks the robot was intended to carry out, while their perception of the robot was not influenced by its appearance, which might affect their attitudes towards it [73]. Additionally, while several aspects were included, the questions used to measure the general acceptance of SAHRs were not completely compre hensive (i.e., they did not include an exhaustive list of tasks that SAHRs could potentially assist with). Finally, the study was carried out within a specific cultural and healthcare sys tem which might hinder generalizability to other cultural settings, considering that other researchers, e.g. [94, 95]., have found that cultural differences might play a consider able role in influencing attitudes toward robots. However, the primary aim of the study was to analyze the factors of acceptance in the specific context where the SAHR will eventually be deployed. Moreover, according to the Special Eurobarometer 460 [89], the general attitude and concerns towards Artificial Intelligence and Robotics in Slovenia are similar to the average across the EU27 and the United Kingdom.

The study aimed to provide an in-depth understanding of the mechanisms that drive professionals’ and patients’ accep tance of SAHRs in hospital environments. The study shows rather clearly that SAHRs are accepted positively among the majority of patients and HCPs who participated in our study; specifically, most participants would agree to be treated or work in a hospital environment where an SAHR operates interdependently with humans. Additionally, the structural models of general acceptance, presented in this paper, point to individual characteristics that contribute to higher acceptance of SAHRs. Namely, among patients, gen eral acceptance depends significantly on the subjective, but realistic, expectations regarding functionalities rather than on fictional views induced by the entertainment industry. On the HCPs` side, which includes nursing and care staff, the fictional view, however, also emerged as a significant (indirect) predictor of the acceptance of SAHRs in hospi tals. This may reflect the general belief that robots, and in hospitals especially humanoid robots, represent a threat to one’s social stability and the ethical treatment of patients However, future research is needed to understand the ori gin of this belief better. Social influences for patients, and ethical acceptability of use and ethical acceptability of human-like interaction for HCPs, have also been identified as some of the key predictors of general acceptance, since the attitudes towards robots were different (i.e., were less favorable) when robots were proposed to carry out activities with a social component. This might indicate that patients and HCPs believe that humanoid robots represent a threat to long-lasting and well-established social relationships between patients and HCPs. To sum up, for a successful implementation of interdependency between robots and HCPs, careful consideration must be carried out regarding the services/tasks an SAHR will carry out or participate in.
